clue.text: Hood imprisoned by stonewall expert? That's soon said

indicators.note: being imprisoned by means one name is shut up inside the other

parts.note: Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson, the Confederate general famed for standing like a stone wall
Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest

explanation.surface: An outlaw is locked up by a man who knows all about obstruction, and the remark is quickly made.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from the idiom 'before you can say Jack Robinson', meaning almost instantly; 'stonewall' points to General Jackson rather than to cricket's defensive batting.
explanation.definitionFit: The name appears in the idiom 'before you can say it', meaning in a moment, so it is a byword for something said in no time.

clue.text: The girl for Narcissus

parts.note: Narcissus in myth loved only himself, but here the word is the plant genus, and the clue asks for a girl's name that is also a member of it

explanation.walkthrough: The capital N makes Narcissus the vain youth of myth; it is really the daffodil genus, one species of which also serves as a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The flower is a species of the daffodil genus, and the word is also used as a girl's given name.

clue.text: No trump hand

parts.note: in bridge and whist there is a special term for a hand of cards that holds not a single trump

explanation.walkthrough: 'No trump' suggests the bridge contract no-trumps; it means a hand containing no trumps at all, for which the old card-table term is the same word as trickery or a racing-circuit bend.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge or whist the term names a hand dealt without any cards of the trump suit.

clue.text: If an author's unlucky the editor's so sad

definitions.text: If an author's unlucky the editor's so sad

parts.words: If an author's unlucky the editor's so sad
parts.note: a rejected author receives a note in which the editor says they decline the work 'with regret'

explanation.walkthrough: The editor's rejection slip conventionally expresses regret, so the editor is, formally at least, sorry.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sorry or sorrowful, the feeling a rejection letter claims on the editor's behalf.

clue.text: He makes one doubly bashful

parts.note: the proverb 'once bitten, twice shy': whoever does the biting leaves the victim shy twice over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubly bashful' is 'twice shy', from the proverb 'once bitten, twice shy', so the person who bites you is the one responsible.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or animal that bites is the cause of the 'once bitten' half of the proverb.

clue.text: Rain oddly enough upset a Nigerian in Kenya

indicators.note: the letters of the word rain are arranged in an odd, unexpected way
in a down clue, upset means the piece is turned upside down, so read from the bottom up

parts.note: the Ibo (Igbo) are a people of south-eastern Nigeria

explanation.surface: Unseasonal rain upsets a visiting Nigerian in East Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges RAIN to NAIR; 'upset' turns IBO into OBI. The definition is the place 'in Kenya', the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the capital of that East African country, so it is found within its borders.

clue.text: Ian appears neatly burdened at the Varsity

parts.note: 'neat' is an old word for cattle, so burdened in a neat way means having an ox on top
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Ian looks smartly weighed down at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neat' (cattle) gives OX and being burdened puts it ON top, so 'neatly burdened' is OX ON, followed by IAN; 'the Varsity' is Oxford, and an Oxonian is a member of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a member or graduate of Oxford University, the varsity of old crossword usage.

clue.text: Toper, unsteady on feet, sees flying monsters

indicators.note: a drunk toper is unsteady on his feet, and the word's letters wobble into a new order

parts.note: a dactyl is a metrical foot of one long and two short syllables

explanation.surface: A drunkard reeling about sees giant flying creatures, as drinkers are said to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsteady' turns TOPER into PTERO; 'feet' are the metrical kind, DACTYLS, not the drinker's own.
explanation.definitionFit: These were winged reptiles of the dinosaur age, monstrous creatures that flew.

clue.text: Smith Minor gets browned off with it

definitions.text: Smith Minor gets browned off with it

parts.words: Smith Minor gets browned off with it
parts.note: a schoolboy, the younger Smith at a boarding school, gets a beating, and also a suntan browns the skin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smith Minor' is the younger of two Smith boys at a British boarding school; the word means both a thrashing he might be fed up with and the browning of skin by the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a beating given to a pupil and the darkening of skin in sunlight.

clue.text: The interminable desk-trays become fewer

indicators.note: without its end, so the word The loses its final letter

parts.note: an office desk has an in-tray and an out-tray

explanation.surface: Endless paperwork in the office trays finally starts to dwindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interminable' cuts THE to TH; the desk-trays are the IN and OUT trays.
explanation.definitionFit: To reduce a crowd or crop in number is to make it sparser, so the phrase means grow fewer.

clue.text: This year it's Addison's

parts.note: the essayist Joseph Addison was born in 1672, so the year of publication marked three hundred years since his birth

explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Addison, the English essayist of The Spectator, was born in 1672; this puzzle appeared in 1972, his three-hundredth anniversary.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a three-hundredth anniversary, which Addison's birth reached in that year.

clue.text: Airy flourish or a duel perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters of or a duel might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A dashing gesture, or perhaps a duel, in a swashbuckling scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the letters of OR A DUEL.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the term is a rapid run of notes, a light ornamental flourish in singing.

clue.text: Better designed for those swinging cats

definitions.text: Better designed for those swinging cats

parts.words: Better designed for those swinging cats
parts.note: plays on the saying 'no room to swing a cat': a place where you could swing one has more space

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'no room to swing a cat' describes a cramped space; a place better suited to swinging cats is more spacious.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means more spacious, having greater space inside.

clue.text: Noted, fine and clear — possible pleasure of retirement in Italy?

definitions.text: Noted, fine and clear — possible pleasure of retirement in Italy?

parts.words: Noted, fine and clear — possible pleasure of retirement in Italy?
parts.note: the Italian phrase for pleasant idleness, which a retired person in Italy might enjoy, begins with a musical term ('noted') for sweetly

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian phrase means 'sweet doing-nothing'; its first word is also a direction in musical notation, which is why the clue says 'Noted'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian phrase means pleasant idleness, the carefree leisure a retired person might enjoy.

clue.text: See 13
Balance nil, 'phone call needed for making it good

parts.note: the balance is what remains, the rest
nil is zero, shown as the letter O
to give someone a ring is to telephone them

explanation.surface: With nothing left in the account, a call to the bank is needed to put things right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balance' is the remainder, not a bank figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Repairing something to its former state is putting it right again.

clue.text: Get a pup in return for this

definitions.text: Get a pup in return for this

parts.words: Get a pup in return for this
parts.note: the letters of 'a pup' read backwards spell the insect stage that is also called by the answer's name

explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'a pup' backwards gives PUPA, the insect stage; the answer is another name for it, so the clue is a cryptic definition rather than wordplay for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the pupa, the encased resting stage of a butterfly or moth.

clue.text: Perhaps a sceptre commands it

indicators.note: signals that the letters of sceptre could be arranged into another word

explanation.surface: A royal staff demands deference from those who see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges SCEPTRE; the whole clue is also the definition, since a sceptre, symbol of royal authority, commands deference.
explanation.definitionFit: Esteem or deference is what a symbol of royal power commands from subjects.

clue.text: I am in Rome at the Academy, from the island

parts.note: Latin, the language of ancient Rome, for 'I am' is sum
taken as written
RA stands for the Royal Academy of Arts in London

explanation.surface: A traveller claims to be in Rome at an art academy, having come from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I am in Rome' means the Latin for I am, not a location.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a large Indonesian island west of Borneo.

clue.text: British king half canonized in the beginning

parts.note: someone canonized is made a saint, abbreviated ST

indicators.note: only the first half of the king's name is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: King Arthur, the legendary British king of the Round Table

explanation.surface: A British king is half made a saint at the start of his reign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps ART of ARTHUR; ST comes first because a saint's title stands before the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The outset of something is its commencement.

clue.text: Be quiet, then split, when heard by a confessor

parts.note: sh is the sound used to tell someone to be quiet
riven is an old past participle meaning split or torn apart

explanation.surface: Told to hush and then torn apart as a priest listens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' looks like a sound signal but belongs to the definition: a penitent whose confession a priest has heard and absolved is shriven.
explanation.definitionFit: Having confessed to a priest and been absolved is the meaning of this old past participle.

clue.text: "Drake he's in his hammock till the great come " (Newbolt)

definitions.text: "Drake he's in his hammock till the great come " (Newbolt)

parts.words: "Drake he's in his hammock till the great come " (Newbolt)
parts.note: a line from Henry Newbolt's poem 'Drake's Drum' with the missing word left as a gap to fill

explanation.walkthrough: Newbolt's 'Drake's Drum' says Drake sleeps until the great Spanish-style invasion fleets come again; the gap is that plural.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means great war fleets, like the Spanish one Drake fought in 1588.

clue.text: Tibetan ox eats sort of mash that Moslem pupils overlook

indicators.note: the ox takes the other letters into its middle, as if eating them

parts.note: a yak is the long-haired ox of Tibet

indicators.note: sort of suggests a version of the word mash, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Tibetan ox munches some kind of mash while schoolchildren look on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' turns MASH into SHMA, which goes inside YAK; the 'pupils' are those of the eyes, which look over the veil.
explanation.definitionFit: The veil worn by some Muslim women covers the face below the eyes, so the eyes look out over it.

clue.text: Small anchor' keeps king over the border

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
an edge is a border or margin

explanation.surface: A small anchor holds a king beyond the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' is a link here; 'over' sets K above EDGE in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a light anchor used for warping a ship along.

clue.text: All in a row

parts.note: people lined up in a row, or the whole crew who row a boat

explanation.walkthrough: 'row' reads as a line but is the verb to propel a boat with oars: everyone who rows.
explanation.definitionFit: The crew members who propel a boat with oars all take part in the rowing.

clue.text: "The ——— dead Did squeak and gibber in the. Roman streets ". (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "The ——— dead Did squeak and gibber in the. Roman streets ". (Hamlet)

parts.words: "The ——— dead Did squeak and gibber in the. Roman streets ". (Hamlet)
parts.note: Horatio's lines in the first act of Hamlet about portents before Caesar's murder, with the missing word left as a gap

explanation.walkthrough: Horatio in Hamlet recalls that before Julius Caesar fell, the dead rose in their burial wrappings and gibbered in Rome's streets; the gap is the word for being wrapped in a shroud.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means wrapped in a shroud or winding cloth, as corpses were for burial.

clue.text: Billy Norman for one

parts.note: William the Conqueror, a Norman called Billy for short, who crossed to England in 1066

explanation.walkthrough: 'Billy Norman' sounds like a person's name; it is William the Conqueror, the Norman who took England in 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: William the Conqueror was an example of someone who attacks and occupies another country.

clue.text: Inmates of museums that are seldom, run on modern lines'

definitions.text: Inmates of museums that are seldom, run on modern lines'

parts.words: Inmates of museums that are seldom, run on modern lines'
parts.note: old railway locomotives now kept in museums rarely run on today's railway lines

explanation.walkthrough: 'run on modern lines' sounds like a museum's management style; it means the exhibits seldom run on today's railway tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Locomotives powered by steam are now mostly museum pieces, rarely seen on modern railways.
